title: The virgin birth and the Greeks’ own stories
source_text: Δοκεῖ μοι οὖν μετρίως κατεσκευάσθαι οὐ μόνον ὅτι γεννηθήσεται ἐκ παρθένου ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι καὶ προφῆται ἦσαν ἐν Ἰουδαίοις, προλέγοντες οὐ μόνον τὰ καθολικὰ περὶ μελλόντων, ὡς τὰ περὶ Χριστοῦ καὶ τὰ περὶ βασιλειῶν κοσμικῶν καὶ περὶ τῶν συμβησομένων τῷ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ περὶ τῶν πιστευόντων τῷ σωτῆρι ἐθνῶν καὶ πολλῶν ἄλλων τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ λεχθέντων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ ἕνα, ὡς περὶ τῶν ὄνων Κὶς ἀπολομένων, πῶς εὑρεθήσονται, καὶ περὶ τῆς νόσου, ἧς ἐνόσησεν ὁ τοῦ βασιλέως Ἰσραὴλ υἱὸς, ἢ εἴ τι ἄλλο ἀναγέγραπται τοιοῦτον. ἔτι δὲ πρὸς Ἕλληνας λεκτέον, ἀπειθοῦντας τῇ ἐκ παρθένου γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ὅτι ὁ δημιουργὸς ἐν τῇ τῶν ποικίλων ζῴων γενέσει ἔδειξεν ὅτι ἦν αὐτῷ βουληθέντι δυνατὸν ποιῆσαι ὅπερ ἐφ᾿ ἑνὸς ζῴου καὶ ἐπ᾿ ἄλλων καὶ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων. εὑρίσκεται δέ τινα τῶν ζῴων θήλεα, μὴ ἔχοντα ἄῤῥενος κοινωνίαν. ὡς οἱ περὶ ζῴων ἀναγράψαντες λέγουσι περὶ γυπῶν· καὶ τοῦτο τὸ ζῷον χωρὶς μίξεως σῴζει τὴν διαδοχὴν τῶν γενῶν. τί οὖν παράδοξον, εἰ βουληθεὶς ὁ θεὸς θεῖόν τινα διδάσκαλον πέμψαι τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων πεποίηκεν ἀντὶ σπερματικοῦ λόγου, τοῦ· ἐκ μίξεως τῶν ἀῤῥένων ταῖς γυναιξὶ, [ποιῆσαι] ἄλλῳ τρόπῳ γενέσθαι τὸν λόγον τοῦ τεχθησομένου: καὶ κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς δὲ τοὺς Ἕλληνας οὐ πάντες ἄνθρωποι ἐξ ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς ἐγένοντο. εἰ γὰρ γενητός ἐστιν ὁ κόσμος, ὡς καὶ πολλοῖς Ἑλλήνων ἤρεσεν, ἀνάγκη τοὺς πρώτους μὴ ἐκ συνουσίας γεγονέναι ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ γῆς, σπερματικῶν λόγων συστάντων ἐν τῇ γῇ· ὅπερ οἶμαι παραδοξότερον εἶναι τοῦ ἐξ ἡμίσους ὁμοίως τοῖς λοιποῖς ἀνθρώποις γενέσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν. οὐδὲν δ᾿ ἄτοπον πρὸς Ἕλληνας καὶ Ἑλληνικαῖς ἱστορίαις χρήσασθαι, ἵνα μὴ δοκῶμεν μόνοι τῇ παραδόξῳ ἱστορίᾳ ταύτῃ κεχρῆσθαι. Ἔδοξε γάρ τισιν οὐ περὶ ἀρχαίων τινῶν ἱστοριῶν καὶ ἡρωϊκῶν ἀλλὰ καὶ περί τινων χθὲς καὶ πρώην γενομένων ἀναγράψαι ὡς δυνατὸν ὅτι καὶ Πλάτων ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀμφικτιόνης γέγονε, κωλυθέντος τοῦ Ἀρίστωνος αὐτῇ συνελθεῖν, ἕως ἀποκυήσει τὸν ἐξ Ἀπόλλωνος σπαρέντα. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ἀληθῶς μῦθοι, κινήσαντες εἰς τὸ ἀναπλάσαι τοιοῦτό τι περὶ ἀνδρὸς, ὃν ἐνόμιζον μείζονα τῶν πολλῶν ἔχοντα σοφίαν καὶ δύναμιν καὶ ἀπὸ κρειττόνων καὶ θειοτέρων σπερμάτων τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς συστάσεως τοῦ σώματος εἰληφέναι, ὡς τοῦθ᾿ ἁρμόζον τοῖς μείζοσιν ἢ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον, ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸν Ἰουδαῖον ὁ Κέλσος εἰσήγαγε διαλεγόμενον τῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ διασύροντα τὴν, ὡς οἴεται, προσποίησιν τῆς ἐκ παρθένου γενέσεως αὐτοῦ, φέροντα τοὺς Ἑλληνικοὺς μύθους περὶ Δανάης καὶ Μελανίππης καὶ Αὔγης καὶ Ἀντιόπης, λεκτέον ὅτι ταῦτα βωμολόχῳ ἔπρεπε τὰ ῥήματα καὶ οὐ σπουδάζοντι ἐν τῇ ἀπαγγελίᾳ.
pass_a_gloss: It seems to me then to have been moderately (μετρίως) established (κατεσκευάσθαι) not only that our Saviour will be born of a virgin but that there were also prophets among the Jews, foretelling not only the general things (τὰ καθολικά) about the future, like those about Christ and those about worldly kingdoms (βασιλειῶν κοσμικῶν) and about what would happen to Israel and about the nations believing in the Saviour and many others of the things said about him, but also the particular (τὰ καθ᾿ ἕνα), as about the asses of Kish that were lost, how they will be found, and about the illness with which the son of the king of Israel was ill, or if anything else such is recorded. Further it must be said to Greeks disbelieving (ἀπειθοῦντας) the birth of Jesus from a virgin, that the Creator (δημιουργός) in the generation of the various animals showed that it was possible for him, having willed (βουληθέντι), to make what [he did] in the case of one animal also in others and in humans themselves. Some female animals are found having no partnership (κοινωνίαν) of a male, as those who wrote about animals say about vultures (γυπῶν); and this animal without mating (μίξεως) preserves the succession (διαδοχήν) of the kinds. What then [is] extraordinary (παράδοξον) if God, wishing to send a divine teacher (θεῖον διδάσκαλον) to the human race, made, instead of a seminal principle (σπερματικοῦ λόγου) from the union of males with women, the principle (λόγον) of the one to be born come about in another way? And according to the Greeks themselves not all humans came from a man and a woman. For if the world is generated/originated (γενητός), as pleased many of the Greeks, it is necessary that the first [humans] came not from intercourse but from the earth, seminal principles having been constituted (συστάντων) in the earth; which I think is more extraordinary than Jesus being born from a half (ἐξ ἡμίσους) similarly to the rest of humans. And nothing absurd to use also Greek stories (ἱστορίαις) toward Greeks, so that we may not seem alone to use this extraordinary story. For it seemed good to some to record, not [only] about some ancient and heroic stories but also about some things that happened yesterday and the day before, as possible, that Plato also was born from Amphictione, Ariston having been prevented from coming together (συνελθεῖν) with her until she bore the one sown (σπαρέντα) from Apollo. But these are truly myths (μῦθοι), having moved (κινήσαντες) to invent such a thing about a man whom they considered to have greater wisdom and power than the many and to have taken the beginning of the constitution (συστάσεως) of his body from better and more divine seeds, as this being fitting for those greater than human (μείζοσιν ἢ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον). But since Celsus introduced the Jew conversing (διαλεγόμενον) with Jesus and disparaging (διασύροντα) the, as he thinks, pretence (προσποίησιν) of his birth from a virgin, bringing the Greek myths about Danae and Melanippe and Auge and Antiope, it must be said that these words befitted a buffoon (βωμολόχῳ) and not one in earnest (σπουδάζοντι) in the report (ἀπαγγελίᾳ).
pass_b_english: It seems to me, then, that a fair case has been made, not only that our Saviour was to be born of a virgin, but also that there were prophets among the Jews. They foretold not only general things about the future, such as those concerning Christ, the kingdoms of the world, what would befall Israel, the nations that would believe in the Saviour, and many other things said about him, but also particular things: how the lost asses of Kish would be found (1 Samuel 9:3–20), the illness from which the son of the king of Israel was suffering (1 Kings 14:1–13), or anything else of the kind on record.

Further, to Greeks who refuse to believe in the birth of Jesus from a virgin, this must be said. In the generation of the various living creatures the Creator showed that, if he willed, he could do in other creatures, and in human beings themselves, what he does in a single kind of creature. Some female creatures are found that have no union with a male, as writers on animals say of vultures; this creature keeps up the succession of its kind without mating. What is so extraordinary, then, if God, wishing to send a divine teacher to the human race, caused the formative principle of the child to be born to come about in another way, instead of through the seminal principle that comes from the union of men with women?

And even by the account of the Greeks themselves, not all human beings were born of a man and a woman. For if the world had a beginning, as many of the Greeks also held, the first human beings must have come into being not from intercourse but from the earth, when seminal principles took form in the earth. And this, I think, is more extraordinary than that Jesus should have been born half in the same way as the rest of humankind.

There is nothing out of place in using Greek stories too in answering Greeks, so that we may not seem to be the only ones to make use of this extraordinary story. For some have seen fit to record, not only about ancient and heroic tales but also about people of yesterday and the day before, that it was possible that Plato too was born of Amphictione, Ariston being prevented from having union with her until she had given birth to the child begotten by Apollo. But these are truly myths, and they moved people to invent such a story about a man whom they thought to have greater wisdom and power than most, and to have received the first formation of his body from higher and more divine seed, since this befits those who are greater than human.

But since Celsus has brought in his Jew arguing with Jesus and ridiculing what Celsus takes to be the pretence of his birth from a virgin, and adducing the Greek myths about Danae, Melanippe, Auge and Antiope, it must be said that such words befitted a buffoon, not a man in earnest about what he reports.

choices.choice: The asses of Kish and the sick son of the king of Israel refer back to the examples of 1.36 (1 Samuel 9:3-20; 1 Kings 14:1-13, Jeroboam's son). 'The kingdoms of the world' may allude to the successive kingdoms of Daniel 2 and 7; uncertain, so not cited inline. The lack of a male among vultures is a commonplace of ancient natural history (compare Aelian, On Animals 2.46); Origen names no author, so no inline source is given. Koetschau brackets [ποιῆσαι] in the sentence on the 'formative principle' as an intrusion; the sentence is read without it. λόγος in that sentence is the Stoic 'seminal principle' (σπερματικὸς λόγος), not the divine Word, and is not capitalised. ἐξ ἡμίσους ('from a half') is rendered 'half in the same way as the rest of humankind': Jesus had a human mother but no human father; the phrasing is compressed. γενητός ('originated', i.e. had a beginning) is the reading printed; the Platonic debate over whether the world had a beginning lies behind it. Amphictione is the name as printed; the usual tradition names Plato's mother Perictione (the Apollo story is told by Diogenes Laertius 3.2, citing Speusippus and others); kept as written. 'Not only... but also' renders οὐ... ἀλλὰ καί. In 'they moved people to invent', the subject of κινήσαντες is the myths. 'What Celsus takes to be' renders ὡς οἴεται. Celsus is reported, not quoted, in this chapter, so no quotation marks are used for him.
ἢ εἴ τι ἄλλο: 'and anything else' -> 'or anything else'
ἀπειθοῦντας: 'who will not believe' -> 'who refuse to believe'
τί οὖν παράδοξον: 'What wonder is it' -> 'What is so extraordinary' (keeps the chapter's key word)
ἐξ ἡμίσους: removed doubled rendering 'from one parent, half in the same way' -> 'half in the same way'; note updated
agency fixed: κινήσαντες agrees with μῦθοι, so 'what moved people ... was that they thought' -> 'they [the myths] moved people to invent such a story about a man whom they thought'
συνελθεῖν 'coming together with' -> 'having union with'; restored 'And' (καὶ ... δέ) before 'even by the account of the Greeks'
